raw_draft.postverify_mechanism:
## Mechanism
**The linkage, per axis.** Balance-sheet tightness: corn carries 15,800 Million Bushels of production against 12,905 Million Bushels of domestic use and 1,567 Million Bushels of carryout [N1][N4][N2]; wheat carries 1,531 Million Bushels of production, 1,099 Million Bushels of domestic use, 717 Million Bushels of carryout [N6][N9][N7]. Dominant driver: on both boards the stocks-to-use ratio is a high-confidence, price-pressuring driver as it rises. Shared macro: a stronger dollar pressures both export programs; crude sits on the corn side through ethanol blend economics.

**The cross-commodity channel itself** is narrow in the tracked model: corn and wheat compete for feed-ration demand, so a higher corn price pulls feed-wheat demand and lifts the wheat-corn spread floor, supporting soft red winter wheat — and the reverse, cheap corn, displaces wheat out of the ration. That is the only feed-side link the model carries; there is no volumetric rationale beyond relative ration cost.

## The record
- Corn stocks-to-use 0.121393 [N13] versus wheat 0.652178 [N14] — each on its own US marketing year, a far wider cushion on the wheat sheet.
- Farm prices: corn $4.8/bu [N5], wheat $6.4/bu [N10] — wheat priced above corn, consistent with corn holding the ration.
- Feed use: corn 151,137 (1000 MT) [N11] against all-wheat 2,177 (1000 MT) [N12] — wheat is the marginal, not the base, feed grain.
- The substitution is documented both ways: corn became the cheaper ingredient and feed use shifted into corn at wheat's expense in MY2021/22 [E1]; and in Vietnam's MY2017/18 corn imports were cut to 6.5 million tons from 7.7 million tons partly on competitive feed wheat from South America and East Europe [E6]. USDA also cut US corn feed and residual by 50 million bushels in 2010/11 on better SRW prospects [E4].
- The season-average farm price for corn rose from $3.56/bu [N24] in MY2019/20 to $4.53/bu [N25] in MY2020/21 — the settled USDA survey actual, not a futures settle.
- Current-window wheat export flow is thin: weekly SRW exports 0 1000 MT [N16], down -30.8 1000 MT week-on-week [N19] and falling in each of the last 2 weeks [N20] — a lagging pace loosens the wheat sheet further.

## Where the record disagrees
The feed-substitution evidence runs in opposite directions across eras, and you should not smooth it: MY2021/22 has corn winning the ration from wheat [E1], while the 2010/11 WASDE has wheat winning it from corn [E4] and the 2017/18 Vietnam read has cheap feed wheat displacing corn imports [E6]. The channel is symmetric and price-set — which grain wins is decided by the spread of the moment, not by a standing hierarchy.

## What to watch
The convex point is not on either flat price but on the spread: wheat's feed bid is roughly linear in the corn price until wheat falls to a feed-equivalent discount, at which point ration-formula substitution switches in a step and wheat feed volume moves non-linearly. Watch the corn-wheat price relationship, US corn ending stocks-to-use, and the SRW export sales pace [N16][N20]. One caveat on dating: the newest dated document here is 2025-09-24, so the substitution episodes above are historical illustrations, not a live read.

## Mechanism
Two separate chains, one shared floor.

- **Palm**: month-end Malaysian inventories are the model's high-confidence loosening driver — a build signals oversupply and pressures the board; a slowing export pace compounds it. That driver is live and quantified here.
- **Rapeseed (MATIF)**: the model's stocks driver is the EU/global rapeseed ending stocks-to-use ratio, high-confidence and loosening when it rises — but no stocks row for it is served on this page. So rapeseed's read runs through the tracked inter-commodity edge: palm sets the floor of the vegetable-oil complex, so a higher palm price lifts rapeseed oil and a softer one withdraws that lift. The two are joined, not opposed.
- **Shared energy leg**: both boards carry a crude-oil driver (biodiesel economics). Brent's five-year z-score stands at 0.507294 z [N1] for palm and the same 0.507294 z [N2] on the rapeseed sheet, up +0.5124 z on the month [N5][N6]. That is one source of risk feeding both — not two.

Net: palm's own balance sheet is the loosening leg; rapeseed has no counter-evidence of its own here, so I lean price-pressuring on palm and follow-the-complex on rapeseed oil, with crude the offsetting support.

## The record
Palm stocks 2.82449 MMT [N3], +0.1966 MMT month-on-month [N7], rising five months running [N8]. Potash, the long-lag cost driver, is at -0.385097 z [N4], -0.0199 z on the month [N9], falling three months running [N10] — the cost-support channel is not firing.

On the 2020-08 to 2021-01 episode window the declared substitution relations were measured. For palm and ICE canola — the graph records these markets stand in for one another in the same use, palm price increases driving up prices across the global vegetable oil market including canola oil: CME palm oil +38.9844 % [N11] in US dollars; ICE canola +27.78 % [N12] in Canadian dollars. Each is a move inside its own settlement currency, US dollars and Canadian dollars, with no exchange rate applied to either figure; the declared relation held on this firing, in-sample on that window only, read on each board's own-currency move, so the currency move sits inside the comparison and is not removed from it. The rate itself: Canadian dollars per US dollar -4.7833 % [N13] over 2020-08-10 to 2020-12-31.

For palm and ZCE rapeseed oil — higher palm oil prices raise rapeseed oil prices through food and blending substitution: ZCE rapeseed oil +17.6352 % [N14] in Chinese yuan against palm's US-dollar move above; each board's figure stays inside the currency its own row names, the relation held in-sample on that window, and the yuan/dollar move sits inside that comparison. Chinese yuan per US dollar -6.2184 % [N15] over the same prints.

For palm and MATIF rapeseed — palm oil price increases lift the entire vegetable oil market including rapeseed oil: that window predates the MATIF board's own price history, so there is no figure to show. That absence is the record's stated limit, not an inference.

For palm and CBOT soybean oil — higher palm prices shift demand to soybean oil: +40.1812 % [N16], relation held in-sample. For palm and CBOT soybeans — higher palm price shifts demand to soybean oil, raising soybean price: +49.5877 % [N17], relation held in-sample.

Dated documents are thin and old for this pair: in January 2018 the USDA reported higher global oilseed ending stocks driven partly by higher Australian rapeseed stocks [E1], and in March 2023 an industry body noted rapeseed and soybean oil filling the sunflower-oil gap [E2]. Neither dates the current stocks position.

## What to watch
- Whether the palm stock build extends a sixth month, or the export pace turns and draws it down — that is the confirming driver on the loosening leg.
- Crude: the energy floor under both boards is the single lever that offsets a palm build; it feeds palm and rapeseed once, not twice.
- For rapeseed specifically, the EU stocks-to-use ratio and EU crush margins — the drivers that would give MATIF a read of its own rather than a borrowed one. No row for them is served here.

## Where the record disagrees
The measured substitution episode and the current stocks panel point opposite ways and are not the same evidence. The 2020-08..2021-01 window records palm and its substitutes rising together [N11][N16][N17] — the complex moving as one. The current panel records palm inventories building for five straight months [N8]. Those are different windows, five years apart; the episode is dated history anchored on its 2021-01-01 end, and the stocks rows are read as of 2026-09-26. Neither overrides the other.

## Mechanism
The link is a substitution pair carried in both directions at high confidence. Palm and soyoil clear the same edible-oil pool and compete for the same biodiesel feedstock slot, so a palm supply loss — drought or heat cutting fresh fruit bunch yields with a two-to-four-quarter biological lag, Indonesian export curbs, or biodiesel diversion — lifts palm, narrows nothing and pushes demand onto soyoil, supporting it. The gate is the soyoil-over-palm premium: a wide premium sends buyers to palm; a narrow one pulls them back to soyoil. That gating is cited, not just modelled — palm ran about 25 percent cheaper than soyoil in MY 2022/23 and consumers shifted into palm [E2], while an earlier balance-sheet read warned that better palm supply prospects weigh on soyoil [E3].

Where it turns convex: soyoil's stocks-to-use buffer is razor-thin [N10], so a demand rotation out of palm lands on a sheet with little cushion and the price response is right-tailed. Palm's own Malaysian cushion [N8] is far larger, which caps how fast palm itself tightens.

## The record
- Malaysian palm month-end closing stocks were 2,824,488 MT on 2026-08-01 [N2] against production of 1,817,499 MT [N1] and exports of 1,294,664 MT [N3] — about 2.18164 months of export cover [N4].
- US soybean oil ending stocks were 833,000 MT on production of 14,048,000 MT for MY2025 [N11][N12], a stocks-to-use ratio of 0.0604982 [N10].
- Indonesian palm sits at 0.176146 stocks-to-use on MY2025 production of 46,700,000 MT [N5][N6].
- Prices: crude palm oil at 1,117 USD/mt and soybean oil at 1,638 USD/mt on 2026-08-01 [N13][N14] — soyoil is the higher-priced leg, and stands 1.21357 sigma above its five-year mean versus palm's 0.269096 [N15][N16]. A governed spread series is not served here, so I will not size the gap.
- Soyoil weekly export commitments printed 0 thousand MT over 2025-09-26..2026-09-26, a change of -0.698 thousand MT on the week [N18][N19]; a lagging export pace loosens that sheet at the margin, and is the one live offset to the tight carryout.

## Cross-commodity
Measured on each commodity's own marketing year, world-basis ratios are comparable as fractions even though the underlying calendars differ:
- CBOT soybean oil, United States MY2025: 0.0604982 [N10]
- CME palm oil, Malaysia MY2025: 0.583039 [N8]
Soybean oil's fundamentals are the tighter of the two and point to firmer prices on any incremental demand; palm's larger Malaysian cushion points the other way, toward softer support until yields or policy draw it down.

## What to watch
- The palm-versus-soyoil price relationship — it is the switch that reallocates Indian and Chinese buying.
- Malaysian month-end stocks and export pace: a stock draw is what converts a palm yield story into a soyoil demand story.
- Indian import-duty settings, already flagged as reducing trade in soy, sunflower and palm oils for MY 2025/26.
- US soyoil export pace off the currently flat print [N18].
